**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 18, 2026
**Re:** Moseth Filtration Media, Inc.: issues under the Soumeir Nonwovens supply arrangement (Delaware law)

---

## I. Executive Summary

Moseth Filtration Media, Inc. ("**Moseth**" or "**Buyer**") buys needle-punched polyester and PPS filter felt rolls from Soumeir Nonwovens, LLC ("**Supplier**"). The governing documents are:

- the Supply Agreement, Effective Date **January 6, 2025**;
- the Order Form (No. MFM-SNW-001);
- the Service Level Schedule;
- a Parent Guaranty from Soumeir Industrial Holdings, Inc. ("**Guarantor**"); and
- Amendment No. 1, dated **September 15, 2026**.

All are governed by Delaware law. Delaware courts enforce clear contract language as written and will not rewrite a bargain to relieve a party of a drafting gap. Most of the issues below therefore have to be fixed by negotiation, not litigation.

I found six substantive issues. In order of urgency:

| # | Issue | Where | Urgency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pending sale of Moseth to Larchfield is a Change of Control needing Supplier's prior written consent, and none has been obtained | Supply Agreement §15.3; Amendment No. 1 Recital C | **High.** Closing is expected Q1 2027 |
| 2 | Product-liability indemnity is now subject to the liability cap because Amendment No. 1 moved it to §10.3 while the carve-out still points to §10.1 | Supply Agreement §11.2(a); Amendment No. 1 §2 | **High.** Baghouse fire and emissions exposure |
| 3 | Chronic-failure termination right for the June 2026 failures lapsed on August 11, 2026, and Amendment No. 1 does not revive it | Service Level Schedule §4.2; Amendment No. 1 Recital B | **High.** Affects leverage in the live dispute |
| 4 | Service Level Schedule measures "Delivery Date" at tender to the carrier, not on arrival, so transit delays escape Service Credits and Critical Delivery Failure counting | Service Level Schedule §1.3; Supply Agreement §1.4, §17.4 | Medium |
| 5 | Supplier's assignment restriction is illusory, so Supplier can assign to anyone, including a Moseth competitor | Supply Agreement §15.2; Parent Guaranty §1.1 | Medium |
| 6 | Automatic three-year renewals, each carrying the $6.2M annual take-or-pay, with only a 30-day opt-out window | Order Form §2.2–2.3, §3.1 | Medium. Window opens about June 2027 |

The two other documents in the folder do not bear on the Soumeir arrangement (see Part IV):

- the Pellingham forklift maintenance agreement; and
- the Rusk Valley outbound freight rate confirmation.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Change of Control from the Larchfield sale requires Supplier's prior written consent, and none has been obtained

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §15.3, §15.1 and §15.4.
- Amendment No. 1 Recital C and §5.2.

**What the documents say:**
- Under §15.3, a "Change of Control of Buyer is deemed an assignment of this Agreement by Buyer and requires the prior written consent of Supplier."
- "Change of Control" means any direct or indirect acquisition of more than 50% of Buyer's voting equity, including by stock purchase.
- If a Change of Control occurs without consent, Supplier may terminate on 30 days' written notice.

Amendment No. 1 Recital C records that Moseth Group Holdings, LLC signed a Stock Purchase Agreement dated **August 28, 2026** to sell **all** of Moseth's equity to Larchfield Capital Partners, L.P. Closing is expected in Q1 2027. That sale is plainly a Change of Control.

**Amendment No. 1 does not contain Supplier's consent or a waiver.**
- The sale appears only in a recital.
- The operative provisions amend §§4.5, 10 and 12.1(a) only.
- §5.2 says the Agreement otherwise remains "unchanged and in full force and effect."
- §17.5 requires any waiver to be in writing and signed by the waiving party.

A recital that acknowledges the deal is not consent to it. Moseth should not treat the Amendment as consent.

**Why it matters:**
- If closing occurs without consent, Supplier can walk away on 30 days' notice. That would cut off Moseth's supply of its core converting input with little time to qualify a replacement for PPS and polyester felt.
- §15.4 makes any assignment in violation of §15 "void." Because a Change of Control is "deemed" an assignment, Supplier may argue the closing itself breaches §15. Moseth would answer that the only stated consequence of an unconsented Change of Control is the §15.3 termination right.
- Supplier currently disputes its liability for the June 2026 failures. It may use the consent request as leverage, for example by demanding concessions on that dispute, or as an exit route.

**Mitigating points:**
- Because §15.3 deems the Change of Control "an assignment ... by Buyer," Moseth has a reasonable argument that the §15.1 standard applies. Under that standard, consent may not be "unreasonably withheld, conditioned or delayed." This is an argument only, since §15.3 itself contains no reasonableness qualifier.
- If Supplier terminates under §15.3, the §13.5 transition right still applies. Moseth could require up to six months of continued supply at then-current prices, because that right is lost only on termination by Supplier under §13.1 or §13.2.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Obtain Supplier's written consent to the Larchfield transaction before closing. Ideally get an express waiver of the §15.3 termination right for this transaction, signed by Supplier.
2. Ask that the consent be unconditional. Do not trade it for concessions on the force majeure dispute.
3. Use the next amendment to soften §15.3 for future transactions. Options include adding a reasonableness standard, excluding financial-sponsor acquisitions, or replacing consent with notice.
4. Coordinate with deal counsel. The Stock Purchase Agreement likely treats this as a required third-party consent, and the timing should be planned around closing.

---

### Issue 2: The product-liability indemnity has fallen inside the liability cap

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §11.1, §11.2(a), §11.3 and §17.4(a).
- Amendment No. 1 §2.1, §2.4 and Recital D.

**What the documents say:**
- Under §11.2(a), the §11.1 cap and the §11.3 consequential-damages exclusion do not apply to "Supplier's obligations under Section 10.1."
- In the original agreement, §10.1 was Supplier's product-liability indemnity. It covers third-party claims for bodily injury, death and property damage, "including fire, explosion or emissions events at any baghouse," as well as defect and nonconformity claims.

Amendment No. 1 changed this structure:
- §2.1 provides that "Section 10.1 is deleted in its entirety." It replaces §10.1 with a narrow intellectual-property infringement indemnity.
- §2.4 restates the product-liability indemnity, word for word, as **new Section 10.3**.
- §2.2 updated the cross-reference in §10.2 to read "Section 10.1 or Section 10.3."
- §11.2(a) was **not** conformed, and there is no general clause saying that references to old §10.1 now refer to new §10.3.
- Under §17.4(a), Amendments prevail over the Supply Agreement.

Read literally, the §11.2(a) carve-out now protects only the IP indemnity. Supplier's product-liability indemnity under new §10.3 is:
- capped at the fees paid or payable in the 12 months before the claim; and
- arguably subject to the §11.3 bar on consequential damages and lost profits.

**Why it matters:**
- A failed felt in a baghouse can cause fires, explosions, emissions exceedances and resulting regulatory fines and customer claims. Those losses can far exceed one year of fees. Annual fees are at least about $6.2M given the minimum commitment.
- The §10.3 indemnity also protects Moseth's customers. Moseth's own downstream indemnity obligations to those customers would therefore be backed only up to the cap.
- Supplier's required products liability insurance is only $5M (§12.1(a), as amended).
- The Parent Guaranty does not help. Under Guaranty §2.4, Guarantor's liability is no greater than Supplier's.

**Arguments Moseth could make if a claim arose before the drafting is fixed:**
- Recital D says the parties wished "to restate Supplier's product indemnity," not to reduce it.
- New Amendment §4 requires insurance covering "Supplier's contractual liability under Section 10," which suggests no intent to narrow coverage.

These points support a scrivener's-error or reformation argument. However, Delaware requires clear and convincing evidence of mutual mistake for reformation. The parties' careful updating of §10.2 also suggests the omission in §11.2 was deliberate, which cuts against Moseth. This is not a position to rely on.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Promptly amend §11.2(a) to read "Supplier's obligations under Sections 10.1 and 10.3" or, more robustly, "Supplier's indemnification obligations under Section 10."
2. Make the amendment effective as of September 15, 2026, so no gap period exists.
3. Add a general interpretive clause stating that cross-references to renumbered or restated provisions follow the restated text.
4. Ask whether Moseth has received the Guarantor acknowledgment due under Amendment §5.3 (see Part III). Get the Guarantor to acknowledge this corrective amendment too.

---

### Issue 3: The chronic-failure termination right for the June 2026 failures has expired

**Where:**
- Service Level Schedule §4.2, read with Amendment No. 1 Recital B.
- Related: Service Level Schedule §§4.3, 5.1 and 5.3; Supply Agreement §§13.3 and 17.5.

**What the documents say:**
- Under Schedule §4.2, if three or more Critical Delivery Failures occur in any rolling 90-day period, Buyer may terminate. That termination may be in whole or as to affected Products, and is without liability and with relief from the Minimum Annual Purchase Commitment under §4.3.
- The right can be exercised only "by written notice to Supplier given **within sixty (60) days after the third Critical Delivery Failure**."
- Amendment No. 1 Recital B records that the third Critical Delivery Failure occurred on **June 12, 2026**.

Sixty days after June 12, 2026 is **August 11, 2026**. The window closed 35 days before Amendment No. 1 was signed on September 15, 2026.

Nothing in Amendment No. 1 tolls, extends, reserves or revives the §4.2 right:
- Its operative terms do not mention the Service Level Schedule except to confirm, in §5.2, that it "remain[s] unchanged."
- §17.5 ("failure or delay in exercising any right is not a waiver") preserves rights that still exist. It does not extend a right with a built-in deadline.

**On the force majeure dispute:**
- Recital B helpfully records that Moseth has notified Supplier in writing that it disputes Supplier's force majeure characterization.
- Under Schedule §5.3, a disputed exclusion counts toward Critical Delivery Failures until the dispute is resolved. The failures therefore counted, and the clock ran, from June 12.
- Moseth's dispute preserves its position on whether the failures were excused. It does not keep the termination window open.

Unless Moseth actually sent a §4.2 termination notice by August 11, 2026, Moseth can no longer terminate for chronic failure based on the June 2026 failures.

**Why it matters:**
- Moseth has lost its cleanest exit. §4.2 termination requires no cure period, carries no liability and reduces the take-or-pay obligation.
- Moseth remains bound to the $6.2M Minimum Annual Purchase Commitment.
- Supplier knows the window has closed, which weakens Moseth's leverage in the force majeure dispute and in the Change of Control consent discussion.

**Recommended fix:**
1. **Confirm the facts.** Determine whether Moseth sent any written notice before August 11, 2026 that could be read as a §4.2 termination notice, and whether any other Critical Delivery Failures occurred after June 12.
   - A later third failure in a different rolling 90-day window starts a new 60-day window.
   - Any such window would have to have opened on or after September 19, 2026 to be open today.
2. **Seek a written extension or waiver from Supplier** reinstating the §4.2 right for the June 2026 failures. This could be bundled into the corrective amendment for Issue 2, or traded against the consent for Issue 1.
3. **Pursue other remedies, preserving the dispute already raised:**
   - Service Credits under Schedule §3, which can be set off under Supply Agreement §5.5.
   - Damages for breach, which are cumulative under §17.8 and §4.4.
   - Termination for material breach under §13.1, after notice and a 30-day cure period, if failures continue.
   - Counting undelivered accepted Purchase Orders toward the minimum under Order Form §3.2(b).
   - Counting substitute purchases toward the minimum under §16.3 if Supplier insists the event was force majeure.
   - If Supplier maintains force majeure lasted more than 45 days, termination under §16.4. Moseth would have to weigh this against its own position that force majeure did not apply.
4. **Diarize future windows.** Implement a docketing process so that any future third Critical Delivery Failure triggers an immediate decision on §4.2 notice.
5. Send a reservation-of-rights letter confirming that the dispute and all other remedies are preserved and that Moseth's signing of Amendment No. 1, which "ratif[ies] and confirm[s]" the Agreement under §5.2, waived nothing.

---

### Issue 4: Conflicting "Delivery Date" definitions mean transit delays escape the service levels

**Where:**
- Service Level Schedule §1.3, used in §§1.4, 1.7, 3.1 and 4.1.
- Supply Agreement §1.4 and §17.4(b).

**What the documents say:**
- Supply Agreement §1.4 defines Delivery Date as the date Products **arrive** at Buyer's Delivery Location and are available for unloading at the dock.
- Service Level Schedule §1.3 defines Delivery Date, "for purposes of this Schedule," as the date Supplier "**tenders the Products to the carrier** at Supplier's facility," as shown on the bill of lading.
- The Schedule uses its definition to measure Late Shipments, On-Time Shipments, the On-Time Delivery Rate, Service Credit tiers and Critical Delivery Failures under §4.1(a) and (b).
- Under §17.4(b), the Service Level Schedule prevails "as to service levels." The shipment-based definition therefore governs measurement.

**Why it matters:**
- Under Supply Agreement §4.1, delivery is DAP and Supplier selects the carrier, who "acts on Supplier's behalf." Supplier therefore bears transit risk commercially, yet transit delays never count against its service levels.
- A shipment can be tendered on time and arrive days late without generating a Service Credit or a Critical Delivery Failure. This reduces Moseth's credits and makes the chronic-failure termination right harder to trigger.
- It may also affect how the June 2026 failures were counted and how the dates in Recital B were calculated.
- Title and risk of loss under §4.3 still pass on arrival, because the Schedule definition is limited to the Schedule. The mismatch matters for performance measurement only.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend Schedule §1.3 to adopt the Supply Agreement §1.4 arrival-based definition, measured by signed proof of delivery at the Delivery Location.
2. Make clear that carrier delays are not an exclusion under Schedule §5.1.
3. In the meantime, request the bills of lading and carrier tracking records under Schedule §6.2. Use them to quantify the late arrivals that are currently uncounted.

---

### Issue 5: Supplier can assign the Agreement to anyone, including a competitor

**Where:**
- Supply Agreement §15.2.
- Parent Guaranty §1.1 and §1.2.

**What the documents say:**
- Supply Agreement §15.2 lets Supplier assign or delegate without Buyer's consent, but only to an assignee that:
  - (a) assumes Supplier's obligations in writing; and
  - (b) has obligations that "constitute Guaranteed Obligations under the Parent Guaranty."
- Parent Guaranty §1.1 defines Guaranteed Obligations as obligations of "Supplier and of **any assignee or transferee of Supplier**."

Condition (b) is therefore satisfied automatically for any assignee. The only real requirement is a written assumption plus notice within 10 business days after the assignment.

**Why it matters:**
- Supplier could assign, without Moseth's consent, to a competitor in filtration media or a vertically integrated bag maker. That assignee would receive Moseth's Buyer Materials, Specifications, forecasts, pricing and customer information.
- The confidentiality obligations in §14 and the protections for Buyer Materials and custom specifications in §9 would bind the assignee. In practice, however, they are a poor substitute for keeping the information away from a competitor.
- The arrangement is one-sided. Moseth cannot assign without Supplier's consent under §15.1, and cannot undergo a Change of Control without it under §15.3.
- The Guaranty's continued coverage is helpful but limited. It keeps the original Guarantor on the hook, but does not protect against operational or competitive harm.
- The guarantor itself can change ownership. Guaranty §7.2 requires notice only if Guarantor stops owning Supplier.
- Partial mitigants:
  - Supply Agreement §6.3 requires Moseth's approval for changes in manufacturing location or process.
  - Supply Agreement §9.3 bars sales of custom-specification Products to third parties.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Amend §15.2 to require Moseth's prior written consent to any Supplier assignment or delegation. A carve-out could allow assignment to Affiliates that remain wholly owned by Guarantor.
2. At a minimum, add:
   - a flat prohibition on assignment to any Moseth competitor;
   - a Moseth termination right, with full §13.5 transition support, on any Supplier assignment or change of control of Supplier or Guarantor; and
   - parity with the restrictions Moseth faces.

---

### Issue 6: Automatic three-year renewals with a narrow 30-day opt-out

**Where:**
- Order Form §2.1, §2.2 and §2.3.
- Order Form §3.1.

**What the documents say:**
- The Initial Term is three years from the Supply Agreement Effective Date of January 6, 2025.
- The Order Form and Agreement then "renew automatically for successive three (3) year Renewal Terms." The only exception is written non-renewal notice given "not more than two hundred ten (210) days and not less than one hundred eighty (180) days" before expiry, which leaves a 30-day window.
- Under §2.3, each Renewal Term carries forward the terms in effect, expressly including the §3.1 Minimum Annual Purchase Commitment of **$6,200,000 per Contract Year**.

On my calculation, if the Initial Term expires on January 6, 2028, the window runs from approximately **June 10, 2027 to July 10, 2027**. The exact dates depend on whether expiry is treated as January 5 or January 6, 2028, so they should be confirmed.

Notices must comply with Supply Agreement §17.3. That means hand, overnight courier or email with confirmation, effective on receipt. A notice sent early is as ineffective as a late one.

**Why it matters:**
- Missing the window, or sending notice too early, commits Moseth to three more years and at least $18.6M of take-or-pay volume. The Agreement has no termination-for-convenience right.
- The window will fall shortly after the expected Larchfield closing. Responsibility for calendaring the notice could be lost in the transition.

**Recommended fix:**
1. Calendar the window now, with reminders in advance.
2. Include it in the Larchfield integration checklist.
3. In the next amendment, negotiate one or more of:
   - a longer and wider notice period, such as notice at any time up to 90 days before expiry;
   - shorter renewal terms of one year;
   - a termination-for-convenience right during any Renewal Term; and
   - a reduced or renegotiated minimum commitment on renewal.

---

## III. Items That Cannot Be Resolved from the Documents

1. **Was any §4.2 notice sent, and were there later Critical Delivery Failures?** The file does not show whether Moseth gave a termination notice by August 11, 2026, or whether failures after June 12 opened a new window.
2. **Merits of the force majeure dispute.** Resolving it requires further facts:
   - whether Supplier gave notice within three business days under §16.2;
   - whether it allocated production under §16.3; and
   - whether the flood was avoidable by reasonable precautions under §16.1.

   We also need Moseth's written dispute notice and Supplier's monthly reports.
3. **Guarantor acknowledgment.** Amendment §5.3 required Supplier to deliver, by about September 29, 2026 (10 business days after the Amendment Date), Guarantor's written acknowledgment that the Guaranty covers the Agreement as amended. We have not seen it. Guaranty §3.3 likely makes the guaranty extend to amendments anyway, but we should obtain the acknowledgment.
4. **Stock Purchase Agreement terms.** We have not reviewed the SPA. It may treat Supplier consent as a closing condition or covenant, and it may allocate the cost of obtaining consent.
5. **Execution.** The copies provided carry no signatures or names. We should confirm that every document was fully executed, including Amendment No. 1.
6. **Contract Year spend and the cap amount.** The current value of the §11.1 cap depends on actual fees paid or payable. We also have not checked whether a Shortfall Amount is likely for Contract Year 2, which ends in January 2027.
7. **Exact term-expiry date.** The precise renewal-window dates in Issue 6 need confirming.
8. **Monthly reports and shipping records.** These are needed to quantify Service Credits and the transit-delay impact under Issue 4.

---

## IV. Documents Reviewed

| Document | Relevance |
|---|---|
| Supply Agreement (January 6, 2025) | Core |
| Amendment No. 1 (September 15, 2026) | Core |
| Parent Guaranty (January 6, 2025) | Core |
| Order Form No. MFM-SNW-001 | Core |
| Service Level Schedule | Core |
| Pellingham Equipment Maintenance Services Agreement (March 3, 2025) | Not relevant. Forklift maintenance at Moseth's Newark facility; no link to the Soumeir arrangement |
| Rusk Valley Outbound Freight Rate Confirmation (October 5, 2026) | Not relevant. Covers Moseth's **outbound** finished-goods freight. Inbound felt deliveries are DAP using Supplier's own carrier under Supply Agreement §4.1, so this document does not affect the delivery-date analysis |

Please let me know if you would like me to draft the consent request to Supplier, the reservation-of-rights letter, or a corrective Amendment No. 2 covering Issues 2 through 6.

2. the Service Level Schedule (as to service levels);
3. the Supply Agreement;
4. the Order Form;

| # | Issue | Location | Urgency |

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Pending sale to Larchfield is a Change of Control requiring Supplier's prior written consent, which has not been obtained

**Where:**
* Supply Agreement §15.3 (Change of Control);
* Amendment No. 1, Recital C; see also Amendment §5.2.

**What the documents say:**
* **SA §15.3.** A "Change of Control of Buyer" is deemed an assignment by Buyer and "requires the prior written consent of Supplier." Change of Control means any direct or indirect acquisition of more than 50% of Buyer's voting equity, including by stock purchase. If a Change of Control occurs without consent, Supplier may terminate on 30 days' written notice.
* **Amendment Recital C.** Moseth Group Holdings, LLC has signed a Stock Purchase Agreement dated August 28, 2026 to sell all outstanding equity of Buyer to Larchfield Capital Partners, L.P. Closing is expected in Q1 2027.
* **Amendment operative terms.** These amend only §§4.5, 10 and 12.1(a). Section 5.2 confirms the Agreement otherwise remains "unchanged." The Amendment contains **no consent to, or waiver of, the Change of Control**.
* **Recital C is not consent.** A recital that acknowledges the transaction does not amount to consent. SA §17.5 requires any waiver to be in a writing signed by the waiving party. Delaware courts generally do not treat recitals as operative terms.

**Why it matters:** The sale is squarely a Change of Control (100% of voting equity, by stock purchase). If it closes without Supplier's written consent:
* Supplier gains a walk-away right on only 30 days' notice. That would leave Moseth without its felt source on very short notice.
* The SA §13.5 six-month transition supply would not be available if Supplier characterizes its termination as a §13.1 breach termination. §13.5 excludes terminations by Supplier under §13.1 or §13.2. Supplier will likely argue that an unconsented Change of Control is a breach.
* Supplier gains negotiating leverage on pricing at exactly the moment Moseth and Larchfield need certainty.
* There may also be SPA implications. Larchfield will likely require this consent as a closing deliverable or as a disclosed exception.

**Recommended fix:**
* Obtain a signed written consent from Supplier, or a waiver of the §15.3 termination right, before closing. It should specifically identify the Larchfield transaction and any pre-closing internal reorganization.
* Ask Guarantor to countersign, or obtain a separate Guarantor acknowledgment that the Guaranty continues for Moseth's benefit after closing (see Guaranty §8.5).
* Argue that the §15.1 standard ("shall not unreasonably withhold, condition or delay") applies, because §15.3 deems a Change of Control to be "an assignment of this Agreement by Buyer." Note the risk: Supplier may argue that §15.3 contains its own standalone consent requirement with no reasonableness qualifier.
* Consider using the consent to negotiate a deletion or narrowing of §15.3 going forward.
* Coordinate with deal counsel on the SPA consent schedule and closing conditions.

---

### Issue 2: Moseth's chronic-failure termination right lapsed on August 11, 2026, and Amendment No. 1 did not revive it

**Where:**
* Service Level Schedule §4.2;
* Amendment No. 1, Recital B.

**What the documents say:**
* **SLS §4.2.** If three or more Critical Delivery Failures occur in any rolling 90-day period, Buyer may terminate "by written notice to Supplier given within sixty (60) days after the third Critical Delivery Failure."
* **Amendment Recital B.** The third Critical Delivery Failure occurred on **June 12, 2026**. Recital B also records Supplier's force majeure position (flooding at its finishing line) and that Buyer "disputes Supplier's characterization of the June 2026 failures as excused force majeure."

**Analysis:**
* Sixty days after June 12, 2026 is **August 11, 2026**. That is 35 days before Amendment No. 1 was signed on September 15, 2026.
* Nothing in the Amendment tolls, extends or reserves the §4.2 right. Section 5.2 states that the Service Level Schedule "remain[s] unchanged."
* By signing Amendment No. 1 in September, Moseth ratified and confirmed the Agreement (§5.2). Supplier will argue this confirms the relationship continues. That argument would weaken any later claim that the lapsed right should be revived on equitable grounds.
* Moseth's written dispute of the force majeure characterization is useful. It preserves Moseth's position that the failures count. Under SLS §5.3, a disputed exclusion counts toward Critical Delivery Failures until the dispute is resolved. But a dispute notice is not a termination notice. Delaware courts enforce contractual notice deadlines as written between sophisticated parties.
* I have seen nothing indicating that a termination notice was sent before August 11.

**Why it matters:** §4.2 was Moseth's cleanest exit. Under SLS §4.3 it carries significant protections:
* no liability for the termination;
* a pro-rata reduction of the $6.2 million Minimum Annual Purchase Commitment;
* no minimum for later periods; and
* transition supply under SA §13.5.

On the documents, that exit is no longer available for the June 2026 failures. Moseth should not proceed as though it can still terminate on that basis.

**Recommended fix:**
* **Confirm the facts.** Verify that no written notice of termination under §17.3 was delivered on or before August 11, 2026. Any document that could be characterized as such a notice should be reviewed (see Part IV).
* **Seek a written extension or waiver.** Ask Supplier for a signed extension of the §4.2 window or a waiver of the deadline. SA §17.5 requires any such waiver to be in writing. This could be bundled with the Change of Control consent negotiation in Issue 1.
* **Preserve the dispute.** Keep pursuing the force majeure dispute under SLS §§5.2, 5.3 and 7.2. Demand Supplier's monthly reports and bills of lading under SLS §§6.1–6.2. Test whether Supplier complied with the notice and allocation conditions in SA §§16.2–16.3. SLS §5.1(a) excuses a shipment only if Supplier complied with those conditions.
* **Consider alternative remedies:**
  * Service Credits for the June Late Shipments (SLS §3) and set-off (SA §5.5).
  * Damages for breach.
  * Termination for material breach under SA §13.1, after notice and a 30-day cure period.
  * If Supplier insists on force majeure, check whether the event lasted more than 45 days. If it did, SA §16.4 gives Buyer its own termination right.
* **Monitor going forward.** Track any new Critical Delivery Failures. A fresh run of three in a rolling 90-day period would open a new 60-day window. Moseth should calendar it strictly.

---

### Issue 3: Amendment No. 1 moved the product-liability indemnity to §10.3, but the cap carve-out still points to §10.1, so the product indemnity is now capped

**Where:**
* Supply Agreement §11.2(a);
* Amendment No. 1 §§2.1 and 2.4.

**What the documents say:**
* **SA §11.2(a), original structure.** The §11.1 cap (fees paid or payable in the preceding 12 months) and the §11.3 consequential-damages exclusion do not apply to "Supplier's obligations under Section 10.1." In the original Agreement, §10.1 was Supplier's broad product indemnity. It covered bodily injury, death and property damage, "including fire, explosion or emissions events at any baghouse," plus product defects.
* **Amendment §2.1.** "Section 10.1 is deleted in its entirety." It is replaced with a narrow IP-infringement indemnity.
* **Amendment §2.4.** The product indemnity is restated, essentially verbatim, as **new Section 10.3**.
* **No conforming change.** The Amendment makes no change to §11.2. It contains no "references to Section 10.1 shall be deemed to refer to Section 10.3" clause. Amendment §1.2 updates only references to "this Agreement." Under SA §17.4, the Amendment controls.

**Analysis:** Read literally, the §11.2(a) carve-out now protects only the IP indemnity. The product-liability indemnity in new §10.3 is subject to:
* the 12-month-fees cap in §11.1; and arguably
* the §11.3 exclusion of consequential damages and lost profits.

Moseth could argue scrivener's error or reformation, because Recital D says the parties intended to "restate" the product indemnity. However, Delaware applies the plain meaning of unambiguous contract text. Reformation requires clear and convincing evidence of mutual mistake. I would not rely on either argument.

**Why it matters:**
* Filter felt failure is a classic cause of baghouse fires and emissions exceedances. Third-party claims from Moseth's industrial end users could far exceed 12 months of fees.
* The Parent Guaranty is no help. Guaranty §2.4 limits Guarantor's liability to the Obligor's liability under the Supply Agreement, so the cap flows through.
* There is an irony in the Amendment. It added a requirement that Supplier's CGL coverage include contractual liability under Section 10 (Amendment §4). So coverage now exists that the cap may prevent Moseth from reaching.
* Before the Amendment was signed on September 15, 2026, the product indemnity was uncapped. Claims arising before that date may still be argued under the original text. That point needs further analysis.

**Recommended fix:**
* Prepare a short Amendment No. 2 that revises §11.2(a) to read "Supplier's obligations under Section 10.1 and Section 10.3," or more simply "Supplier's obligations under Section 10."
* Add a general clause providing that cross-references to renumbered or relocated provisions follow the relocated text.
* Make the change retroactive to September 15, 2026.
* Have Guarantor acknowledge the change. This could be included in the acknowledgment due under Amendment §5.3.

### Issue 4: The assignee-guaranty condition on Supplier assignment is illusory, so Supplier can assign to anyone, including a Moseth competitor

**Where:**
* Supply Agreement §15.2;
* Parent Guaranty §§1.1 and 1.2.

**What the documents say:**
* **SA §15.2.** Supplier may assign or delegate without Buyer's consent to an assignee that (a) assumes Supplier's obligations in writing and (b) whose obligations "constitute Guaranteed Obligations under the Parent Guaranty."
* **Guaranty §1.1.** "Guaranteed Obligations" means the obligations under the Supply Agreement "of Supplier and of any assignee or transferee of Supplier." Guaranty §1.2 makes any such assignee an "Obligor."

**Analysis:**
* Because the Guaranty automatically covers every assignee, condition (b) is satisfied for any assignee at all. The only real condition is a written assumption.
* Supplier can therefore assign or delegate to any third party without Moseth's consent. That includes a filter-media competitor or a weak manufacturer. Supplier only has to notify Moseth within 10 business days *after* the assignment takes effect.
* By contrast, Moseth's own assignments, and its Change of Control, require Supplier's consent (§§15.1, 15.3).

**Why it matters:**
* **Confidential information.** An assignee would receive Moseth's Buyer Materials: specifications, forecasts, pricing and customer information (§1.12). It would also receive the custom Specifications protected by §9.3. Confidentiality obligations (§14) would bind the assignee, but a competitor's possession of that information is itself the harm.
* **Guaranty credit.** The Guaranty still backstops performance. But Guarantor's practical ability to perform through a competitor's or stranger's facility is untested. Guaranty §2.2 contemplates substitute supply only from Guarantor's own facilities.
* **No protection on a sale of Supplier.** Guaranty §7.2 requires only notice if Guarantor sells Supplier. Supplier has no change-of-control restriction at all.

**Recommended fix:**
* Amend §15.2 to require Moseth's prior written consent to any Supplier assignment or delegation. Moseth could agree that consent will not be unreasonably withheld, except for assignments to Guarantor's wholly owned subsidiaries that remain guaranteed.
* At a minimum, add a flat prohibition on assignment or delegation to any person engaged in the filtration media or filter bag business in competition with Moseth.
* Consider requiring advance notice of any assignment.
* Consider adding a Supplier change-of-control trigger that gives Moseth a termination right with transition supply.

### Issue 5: Conflicting "Delivery Date" definitions; the Service Level Schedule's shipment-based definition controls and excludes transit delays

**Where:**
* Service Level Schedule §1.3;
* Supply Agreement §1.4;
* SA §17.4(b) (order of precedence).

**What the documents say:**
* **SA §1.4.** "Delivery Date" is the date Products "arrive at Buyer's Delivery Location," meaning when they are available for unloading at Buyer's dock.
* **SA §4.1.** Delivery is DAP Moseth's dock, with Supplier selecting the carrier, which "acts on Supplier's behalf."
* **SA §4.3.** Title and risk pass on arrival.
* **SLS §1.3.** "For purposes of this Schedule," Delivery Date means the date Supplier "tenders the Products to the carrier at Supplier's facility," as shown on the bill of lading.
* **SA §17.4(b).** The Schedule prevails "as to service levels."

**Analysis:** The SLS definition drives every service-level metric: Late Shipment, On-Time Shipment, On-Time Delivery Rate, Service Credits, and the "no Delivery Date" trigger for Critical Delivery Failures in SLS §4.1(a). Given SA §17.4(b), the shipment-based definition governs. As a result, a load that leaves Supplier's dock on time but arrives late because of Supplier's own carrier:
* is an On-Time Shipment;
* earns no Service Credit; and
* never counts toward a Critical Delivery Failure.

This happens even though the Required Date is the delivery date requested in Moseth's Purchase Order. Moseth plainly means that date as an arrival date.

**Why it matters:**
* Moseth's credits are understated.
* Chronic-failure termination becomes harder to trigger.
* Supplier controls the carrier, so the definition rewards Supplier for poor transit performance it could manage.
* This may also bear on the June 2026 count. Supplier's monthly reports may have measured the June shipments on a tender basis.

**Recommended fix:**
* Conform SLS §1.3 to SA §1.4, measuring by arrival at the Delivery Location. Alternatively, delete SLS §1.3 so the Agreement definition applies.
* Confirm that the Required Date is an arrival date.
* Require Supplier's monthly reports (SLS §6.1) to show both the tender date and the arrival date for each Shipment.
* In the meantime, request the June 2026 bills of lading and carrier tracking records under SLS §6.2 and recompute the June metrics on both bases.
